Three parameters carve the construct: (1) domain — the object is the sound structure of a language at and below the level of the word: the inventory of distinctive sound units (the phoneme system), their contextual variants (allophones), and the constraints and rules on their combinations (phonotactics, assimilation, stress, tone); the domain's boundaries are set by the level of analysis — the physical and perceptual description of speech sounds belongs to phonetics, the decomposition of words into morphemes belongs to morphology, and meaning belongs to semantics; (2) method — analysis proceeds by contrasting minimal pairs to isolate the distinctive units of a language, by describing the phonetic variants that surface in specific contexts, and by stating the rules that map an underlying representation onto its surface form; (3) codification — findings are fixed as phonemic inventories, phonotactic constraints, and rule statements that differ per language but share a stable descriptive form. Phonology persists as a discipline: it is taught as a field of linguistics, its categories (phoneme, allophone, phonotactics, stress, tone) form the stable vocabulary of grammatical description across languages, and its methods are operationalized in dictionaries, speech technology, and language documentation. payload.body: An allophone is a human-made phonological category — the contextual variant of a phoneme: the particular surface realization that a language's phonology assigns to a phoneme in a specific phonetic environment, without changing word meaning. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) identity anchoring — every allophone is indexed to a phoneme; it is that phoneme's surface form in a given context, so the allophone set of a language is the variant set of its phoneme inventory (in English, /p/ is realized as aspirated [pʰ] at the start of a stressed syllable, as in 'pin', and as unaspirated [p] after /s/, as in 'spin'); (2) distribution — the allophones of a phoneme occur in complementary distribution, their environments not overlapping, which is exactly what separates a predictable variant from a contrastive phonemic pair; free variation, where two variants share an environment without changing meaning, is the boundary case the category is carved against; (3) predictability — the variant is determined by environment according to the language's phonological rules and can be predicted from context, unlike phonemic choice, which is selected for meaning. The boundary with phonetics is set by the level of analysis: the physical and auditory description of the variant belongs to phonetics; what is carved here is the phonological category of the variant within a language's sound system. The codification mechanism is the transcription convention itself: the phoneme is written in slashes /p/ and its allophonic realizations in square brackets [pʰ], so the distinction is carried in every phonological description. Allophones persist as a discipline's standing category: taught in phonology curricula, fixed in the phonemic inventories and rule statements of language description, and operationalized in speech technology and language documentation. payload.body: Cybernetics is a human-made science — the study of communication and control in animals and machines, in Wiener's own subtitle. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) subject matter — cybernetics addresses communication and control systems wherever they occur: the nervous system, the thermostat, the feedback amplifier, the fire-control radar; its core concept is feedback — the correction of a system's behavior by an error signal — and it treats biological and mechanical controllers as instances of one formal kind, so 'communication' and 'control' name the same underlying mechanism; (2) founding and method — founded in Norbert Wiener's Cybernetics: Or Concerning Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine (1948), the discipline arose from the wartime convergence of information theory, physiology, statistics, and engineering practice, and its method is the mathematical modeling of feedback loops, stability, and noise; (3) transmission — cybernetics persists as a discipline: textbooks and journals (from von Foerster's Kybernetik onward), engineering practice (automatic control, servomechanisms, signal processing), and its theoretical descendants — systems theory, second-order cybernetics (Maturana, Varela, von Foerster), and the feedback vocabulary that fields as distant as economics and ecology still borrow. Boundaries: it is not information theory (the source it drew on), not engineering control theory (the sibling it fed), and not systems theory (the descendant that generalized it) — cybernetics is the feedback-based study of communication and control spanning living and machine. [formal: kybernetike | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.35]

Three parameters carve the construct: (1) constraint scope: the object is the inventory of permissible phoneme sequences in a language, including onsets (initial consonant clusters), codas (final consonant clusters), and syllable structure — for example, English permits /str-/ at word onset but not /ŋ-/ or /vn-/; Japanese restricts syllable structure to (C)V, allowing at most a single consonant-vowel nucleus with optional coda; (2) language-relativity: what counts as permissible in one language may be impossible in another, since the phonotactic constraints of each language form a distinct system that speakers internalize as unconscious knowledge — a sequence that is a well-formed word in one language may be impossible or trigger repair strategies in another; (3) descriptive form: phonotactics is expressed as constraints on phoneme sequences, typically stated as production rules, feature-based restrictions, or probabilistic models that map which transitions between phonemes are licensed in which positions. Phonotactics persists as a descriptive tool: it is taught as part of phonological analysis, codified in dictionaries that include phonetic transcriptions, and operationalized in speech synthesis, speech recognition, and language documentation to constrain the generative space of possible word forms.

payload.body: Phonotactics is a human-made phonological category — the set of rules that govern which sound combinations are permissible in a language and where they may occur. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) constraint scope: the object is the inventory of permissible phoneme sequences in a language, including onsets (initial consonant clusters), codas (final consonant clusters), and syllable structure — for example, English permits /str-/ at word onset but not /ŋ-/ or /vn-/; Japanese restricts syllable structure to (C)V, allowing at most a single consonant-vowel nucleus with optional coda; (2) language-relativity: what counts as permissible in one language may be impossible in another, since the phonotactic constraints of each language form a distinct system that speakers internalize as unconscious knowledge — a sequence that is a well-formed word in one language may be impossible or trigger repair strategies in another; (3) descriptive form: phonotactics is expressed as constraints on phoneme sequences, typically stated as production rules, feature-based restrictions, or probabilistic models that map which transitions between phonemes are licensed in which positions. Phonotactics persists as a descriptive tool: it is taught as part of phonological analysis, codified in dictionaries that include phonetic transcriptions, and operationalized in speech synthesis, speech recognition, and language documentation to constrain the generative space of possible word forms.
